title: Detection of Upload Malware
summary: This detection strategy covers uploading malware, the technique where an adversary stages a payload on infrastructure they control, such as a public file sharing service, a code hosting repository, a cloud storage bucket or a web shell on a compromised site, so that it can be downloaded by the victim later. It matters because the upload step is the first point in the chain where the defender can see the adversary's own infrastructure being used, and blocking it removes the payload before delivery. The telemetry that makes it possible is cloud storage and file sharing audit logs, code repository push events, web server logs showing unexpected script creation on a hosted site, proxy logs for uploads to file transfer services, and antivirus or sandbox results on files that later reach the estate. Detection fails because uploads to public hosting are made by ordinary employees every day, and because the adversary often uploads with an account the victim cannot see.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for malware being placed on storage that the attacker controls. The attacker uploads the file first and delivers it later. The rule watches for uploads of suspicious files to public hosting. It also watches for new scripts appearing on your own web servers.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attack needs somewhere to keep its tools. Public file hosts are cheap and hard to block. If you catch the upload, the later download has nothing to fetch. The upload often happens from an account that is already compromised, which is a second warning.
howItWorks: Cloud storage and file sharing services record each upload. The record holds the account, the file name, the size and the sharing settings.
Code hosting services record push events, which list the files added to a repository.
Your web servers record file creation under their document directories, including script file types.
The security monitoring platform collects these records and enriches file names with hash and reputation data.
The rule selects uploads of executable or script file types, or new scripts in web directories.
It ranks findings by whether the account, the file type and the destination are new for that user.
beginner.example: Think of a courier who leaves a parcel in a locker at the station. The parcel is not delivered yet. The courier collects it later and carries it to your door. If the station staff notice the strange parcel, the delivery never happens. This detection watches the locker.
takeaways: The staging upload is a rare chance to see attacker infrastructure in use.
Watch your own web servers for unexpected scripts, because that is staging too.
File type and destination novelty separate a real staging upload from daily file sharing.

objectives: Define staging and the upload malware step in the delivery chain.
Identify the cloud, repository, web server and proxy telemetry that records uploads.
Write a rule that selects script and executable uploads by account and destination.
Describe how to use file reputation services without blocking normal work.
Explain how blocking a staged payload affects the rest of the attack chain.
dataSources: Cloud storage and file sharing audit logs recording upload events with account, object name, size and sharing scope
Code repository push events listing new files, commit author and the repository visibility setting
Web server and content management system logs recording creation of script files in public directories
Secure web gateway logs for uploads to file transfer and paste services with file name and size
Malware sandbox and reputation service results for file hashes observed in upload or download telemetry
logic: The pattern is an upload of an executable, archive or script file to an external file sharing service, code repository or personal storage account, or the sudden appearance of a new script file in a web server directory, performed by an account that has no history of this activity or from an address that does not match the account's usual location. The fields that must be correlated are the uploading account and source address, the destination service or web directory, the object name and extension, the object size and hash, the sharing permission applied, and the account's upload baseline. The benign case is a developer pushing source code to an approved repository with a matching identity and a normal commit pattern, or an employee sharing a spreadsheet through the company file service; the malicious case is an upload of a renamed binary or a web shell to a public service or to a writable web directory, often with public sharing enabled, shortly after an authentication from an unusual address.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Script or Executable Upload to External File Service
# logsource:
#   product: aws
#   service: s3
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: 'PutObject'
#     object_name|endswith:
#       - '.exe'
#       - '.dll'
#       - '.ps1'
#       - '.js'
#       - '.zip'
#   filter_approved:
#     bucket|endswith:
#       - 'release-artifacts'
#       - 'approved-build-output'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved
# level: high
falsePositives: Software build pipelines that publish installers and archives to a release bucket on every merge
Developers who upload test scripts and sample packages to a personal cloud drive while working remotely
A web team that uploads template and script files to a corporate site through a content management system
An employee who shares a compressed folder of documents with an external partner through a public file service
tuningNotes: Allow list the buckets, repositories and service accounts used by build and release pipelines, then require the upload to come from an identity outside those pipelines before alerting. Enrich every candidate with a hash lookup so files already known and approved are dropped automatically. Scope the web server part of the rule to writable public directories and to file types the site platform never creates. Because an attacker may upload from infrastructure you cannot see, keep a second rule on outbound downloads of script and executable files from newly registered domains by user workstations, and accept that the upload side only covers staging that touches your own accounts.
